title: The Brain Paradox: Four Simple Cards Fool Ninety Percent
description:
Myth vs. Neural Mechanism — Peter Wason (1966/1968): The Four-Card Puzzle ('E — K — 4 — 7') That Stumps 90% of Educated Adults, grounded in P. C. Wason (1968) (Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology). Empirical findings show that in 1966-1968 at University College London, Peter Wason laid FOUR double-sided cards flat on a table — showing E, K, 4, and 7 (or D, K, 3, 7) — with one guarantee: every card has a letter on one side and a number on the other.

Follow-up physiological and behavioral evidence demonstrates: Participants had to test ONE simple rule by turning over ONLY the minimum necessary cards: 'If a card has a vowel on one side, then it has an even number on the other side.'.

Primary Peer-Reviewed Sources:
- P. C. Wason (1968). Reasoning about a Rule. Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1080/14640746808400161
- Peter C. Wason (1969). Regression in Reasoning? British Journal of Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.2044-8295.1969.tb01221.x
- P. N. Johnson-Laird, Paolo Legrenzi, Maria Sonino Legrenzi (1972). Reasoning and a Sense of Reality. British Journal of Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.2044-8295.1972.tb01287.x
